title: Hugging Face's New AI Biology Model Lets You Chat with DNA
content:
The AI platform Hugging Face on Thursday released a new open-source model for understanding DNA that can run locally on a laptop.
Developed in collaboration with researchers at Zhongguancun Academy in China and the University of Naples Federico II in Italy, the model is trained on genomic sequences and natural language so that people can ask questions about the effects of DNA changes on gene activity and health and get conversational answers in return.
Lewis Tunstall, a senior research scientist at Hugging Face, says the tool is meant to help researchers design new drugs and genetic therapies, and it could potentially aid patients in interpreting their own genomes.
“We've unlocked a new capability in language models, which is fundamentally about being able to chat with DNA,” he says of the new model, dubbed Carbon-X. Using natural language means even nontechnical users “can actually ask questions about DNA that wouldn't be accessible through any other tool.”
Known as essentially GitHub for AI models, Hugging Face provides a library of readymade AI tools and a platform for running primarily open-weight and open-source AI applications for developers, researchers, businesses, and people who want to experiment with AI without building everything from scratch. In September, Nvidia agreed to acquire the company for nearly $13 billion. (Hugging Face was also at the center of a major hack by OpenAI’s models earlier this year.)
DNA is more like computer code than natural language. Instead of 0s and 1s, though, it uses As, Cs, Gs, and Ts to encode information. A human genome contains 6 billion of these letters. While the human genome has been sequenced end to end, scientists still don’t understand how most of it works.
Now, AI models are helping researchers decipher some of those mysteries. Last year, Google DeepMind released AlphaGenome, which predicts the effects of DNA sequences and genetic mutations but does so in a numeric format. It also requires more compute power. Evo 2, a model developed by the Arc Institute and Nvidia, along with academic partners, speaks the language of DNA and can generate entire genomes from scratch.
Carbon-X integrates both DNA and natural language in a conversational interface. Think of it like a ChatGPT for DNA.
The team started with an existing language model and expanded its vocabulary to read DNA in groups of six letters. They then continued training on 300 billion chunks of data, or tokens, that combined DNA sequences, English text, and examples linking DNA to biological descriptions. The DNA sequences came from mammals (including humans), other vertebrates, invertebrates, plants, fungi, and protozoa. Tunstall says the team didn’t train the model on viruses because they didn’t want it to be used for potentially dangerous applications.
Users won’t be able to upload full human genomes. The model was trained to be able to ingest DNA sequences of roughly 50,000 base pairs, so users will only be able to query small parts of the genome at a time.
One of the ways scientists could use Carbon-X is to help understand whether a genetic mutation is benign or disease-causing, a key step in developing a targeted drug or genetic therapy. If an intervention targets the wrong mutation, it could be totally ineffective or, worse, cause unintended harm.
Researchers face restrictions when it comes to uploading identifiable or sensitive patient data to frontier AI models, so Tunstall says his team intentionally designed a small model with 14 billion parameters. That will allow it to run locally on the user’s hardware, rather than rely on cloud-based models. No data is sent to Hugging Face or any other company, he says.
The developers of Carbon-X caution that they haven’t validated the model yet with actual wet lab experiments, so they can’t say how accurate its predictions are.

report.summary: Hugging Face has released Carbon-X, an open-source 14-billion-parameter AI model that lets users ask questions about DNA in plain language and run it locally on a laptop.
report.background: Hugging Face is essentially the GitHub of AI, hosting open-weight models and tools for developers, researchers and companies — Nvidia agreed to acquire it for nearly $13 billion in September. Genomics is an obvious next frontier: DNA is code, but written in 6 billion A/C/G/T letters, and while the human genome is fully sequenced, scientists still do not understand what most of it does. AI labs have started chipping away — Google DeepMind's AlphaGenome predicts mutation effects numerically but is compute-hungry, while the Arc Institute and Nvidia's Evo 2 can generate genomes from scratch. Carbon-X, built with Zhongguancun Academy in China and the University of Naples Federico II, pushes in a different direction: pairing genomic sequences with natural language so the questions can be asked by anyone, not just bioinformaticians with pipelines.
key_points: Carbon-X behaves like a ChatGPT for DNA. The team took an existing language model, expanded its vocabulary so it reads DNA in six-letter chunks, then continued training on 300 billion combined tokens of DNA sequence, English text and examples linking genetic changes to biological descriptions. Users ask about mutations in plain English and get conversational answers.

It is deliberately small and local. At 14 billion parameters, the model is designed to run on a user's own laptop or workstation rather than in the cloud, so no patient or research data is sent to Hugging Face or anyone else — a direct answer to the restrictions researchers face when uploading identifiable genomic data to frontier models.

Training data spans mammals including humans, other vertebrates, invertebrates, plants, fungi and protozoa. Viruses were intentionally left out to reduce the risk of dangerous applications, and the model only handles roughly 50,000 base pairs at a time — so users cannot upload a whole human genome, only small regions.

The intended killer app is variant interpretation: judging whether a genetic mutation is harmless or disease-causing before designing a drug or gene therapy. Targeting the wrong mutation can make a treatment useless or actively harmful, so a fast conversational triage tool could save real lab time.

Accuracy is unproven. The developers say they have not yet validated the model with wet-lab experiments, so nobody can say how reliable its predictions are — a critical caveat for anyone tempted to use it clinically.
report.impact: For the AI industry, Carbon-X is another signal that open-weight, locally runnable models are moving into scientific domains once dominated by big-cloud systems — and that small, domain-specialised models can compete with far larger ones on usability. It also shows continued US-China-EU academic collaboration at a time when AI geopolitics is tense. For developers, it is a template: fine-tune an existing LLM, extend the tokenizer for a non-text alphabet, and ship it as open weights. For researchers and clinicians, a plain-language DNA interface dramatically lowers the barrier to genomic analysis, potentially speeding target validation for drugs and gene therapies. For regular users, the promise of interpreting your own genome is real but premature — without wet-lab validation, conversational answers about your DNA should be treated as hypotheses, not diagnoses.
report.tools: Watch the Carbon-X model card on the Hugging Face Hub (the weights should be downloadable for local inference via Transformers or llama.cpp-style runtimes). For comparison, try Google DeepMind's AlphaGenome API for numeric variant-effect predictions and the Arc Institute's Evo 2 for genome generation. The Nucleotide Transformer family on Hugging Face offers another open DNA-LLM baseline, and AlphaFold 3 or Boltz-1 complement these when you need protein structure downstream of a variant.
